hasegawa-two-step-method: Section 2.3, p.5: the authors define their own method as two steps, kernel learning then classification with the learned kernel. Read in context with Section 2.4 and 2.5.
hasegawa-objective-labels: Section 2.3, p.5, after Eq. (5): the authors set Fi(x,x') = yy' for the classification task and explain the effect. Their own choice of objective.
hasegawa-rbm-size-embedding: Section 2.5, p.7 and the Figure 2 caption: node counts {10,4,4}, D-Wave Advantage, and the eight-qubit bipartite subgraph embedding are stated as the experimental setup. The authors are Tohoku University, SCSK and Sigma-i, not D-Wave staff, so this is not a vendor claim.
hasegawa-synthetic-setup: Section 3, p.9: x ~ N(0, I_d), label from the sign of a norm threshold, d = 10, 1000 train and 1000 test samples. The paper's own data setup.
hasegawa-sampling-count: Section 3, p.9: 500 RBMs embedded at once on D-Wave Advantage, two samples per embedding, 1000 samples in total. The paper's own sampling setup.
hasegawa-baselines-config: Section 3, pp.9-11 (Table II bullet and the Figure 3 discussion): RKS with IKL settings (MLP 10 -> (4,4) -> 10, batch 200, 200 and 1000 random features) and Optuna tuning of mean and variance for Gaussian RFF are stated as the baseline configuration. Setup only, not a result.
hasegawa-classifier-regularization: Section 2.5, p.9 (end of the section): kernel perceptron, with regularization so that the size of alpha does not exceed 0.5. The paper's own classifier setup.
hasegawa-model-size-limit: Discussion and Conclusion, p.14: the authors say validation used a model size easily run on a quantum annealer and that larger models and broader datasets are future work. A limit the paper states about its own work.
hasegawa-hidden-nodes-open: Discussion and Conclusion, p.14: the authors name the link between hidden-layer size and the distribution of omega as a future topic, and say prediction accuracy needs to be investigated. A stated open problem of their own work.
hasegawa-binary-scope: Section 1, p.3: the paper states it demonstrates the method on binary classification with synthetic data and Fashion MNIST. This is the scope of its experiments.
fashion-mnist-setup: Section 3, p.9: 1000 images from each of two classes, PCA from 784 to 10 dimensions, 500 RBMs embedded on D-Wave Advantage. The paper's own experimental setup.
no-speedup-guarantee: Discussion and Conclusion, p.14: the authors state their method lacks mathematical guarantees for quantum speedup and that speedup by the annealer as a sampler remains to be clarified. A limit stated about their own method.
hassanshahi-simulated-exact-kernel: Section 1, p.2 and Section 3.2, p.4: the kernel matrix was computed exactly from the simulated wave function, equal to infinite shots on a noiseless device. The paper's own simulation setup.
hassanshahi-qubits-equal-features: Section 3.2, p.4: following the Havlicek circuit family, the number of qubits equals the number of features. The paper's own circuit setup.
hassanshahi-data-labels-features: Section 2, pp.2-3: Galaxy Zoo 1 data, spiral or elliptical label if more than 80% of debiased votes, five distance-independent features from the Barchi et al. catalogue. The paper's own data setup.
hassanshahi-kgal-splits: Section 2, p.3: split into Kgal >= 5, >= 10 and >= 20, one classifier each, following Barchi et al., with Kgal not used as an input feature. The paper's own data setup.
hassanshahi-kernels-compared: Section 4, p.4: RBF classical kernel, quantum circuits with single-qubit rotations then two-qubit interactions between all pairs, hyperparameters by grid search maximising ROC AUC. The paper's own method setup.
hassanshahi-cv-uncertainty: Section 6, p.7 (and the Figure 7 caption, p.5): the paper defines the quoted uncertainty as the standard deviation of the 5-fold cross-validation scores. A definition of its own reported quantity.
hassanshahi-comparison-caveats: Section 4, p.5: the authors say the comparison with Barchi et al. might not be fair and list three differences (training size limited by quantum kernel cost, 5-fold CV against an 80-10-10 split, optimised ROC AUC against a possibly different score). A caveat stated about their own comparison.
hassanshahi-device-error-handling: Section 4, Running on hardware, p.6: dynamical decoupling for suppression, T-REx for mitigation, and a simplified kernel circuit with two-qubit gates only between nearby qubits to avoid Swap gates. The paper's own hardware setup.
hassanshahi-device-dataset-setup: Section 4, Running on hardware and the Table 2 caption, pp.6-7: 50 spirals and 50 ellipticals, 4-fold cross-validation, 75 train and 25 test, 4000 shots per kernel-entry circuit. The paper's own device-run setup.
hassanshahi-noise-caveat: Section 6, p.7: the authors state that further investigation of noise contributions could indicate worse time complexity and reduced performance for the quantum algorithm. A caveat stated about their own work.
hassanshahi-future-work: Section 6, p.7: the authors name a larger or different feature set, encoding relations between features, and multi-class classification as open, and note qubits equal features. Open problems stated about their own work.
hassanshahi-advantage-open: Section 5, discussion paragraph after Figure 10 (anchored p.7 by the reader and p.6 by the stored record; the page break sits near this passage): the authors say practical quantum advantage is an open question, that added overhead could reject it, and that the study is a proof-of-concept.
haug-rm-total-measurements: Section IV, p.3: the authors define their own procedure (r random bases, s samples each, L states) and state the total NR = srL. The count follows from that procedure.
haug-rm-exponential-in-qubits: Section IV, p.3: the authors state the NR proportional to 2^(aN) L scaling (taken from refs [41,42]) as the cost of their own method, say it is prohibitive for large N and moderate near ten qubits. A limit the paper states about its own method.
haug-conventional-quadratic: Section IV, pp.3-4 and Appendix B/D, p.11: the swap and inversion tests prepare both states per kernel entry, so the paper's own cost formula sc Ltrain(Ltrain-1)/2 + sc Ltrain Ltest is quadratic in L. Stated as the cost model the paper compares against, not as a proved bound.
haug-encoding-definition: Section III, p.2, Eq. (2) and the Figure 1 caption: the paper defines its own encoding theta_i = theta_r + c x_i into a hardware-efficient PQC with N qubits and d layers.
haug-features-linear-depth: Figure 1 caption, p.2: one feature per single-qubit rotation parameter, so the feature count is linear in N and d (M = N(d+1) for the NPQC, Appendix A). Follows by construction from the paper's own encoding.
haug-kernel-fidelity-definition: Section III, p.2, Eq. (3): the paper defines its own quantum kernel as Tr(rho_i rho_j), which reduces to the squared overlap for pure states.
haug-yzcx-definition: Section III, p.3 and Appendix A, p.11: the paper defines YZ-CX as d layers of y and z rotations then CNOTs on a chain. The text layer prints 'F = I' but the rendered page 3 shows 'F not equal I' (a lost slash), so the value is right. Numerical QFIM in the Figure 7 caption supports it.
haug-rm-procedure: Section IV, p.3, Eq. (7): the paper describes its own measurement procedure (Haar-random single-qubit bases, s samples, Hamming-distance weighted sum), following ref [42]. A definition of its own method.
haug-depolarizing-mitigation-method: Section V, p.4, Eq. (8): the paper defines its own mitigation: purity from the same randomized data, p_i from a quadratic equation (refs [23,47]), and division by the square root of the purity product. The value states what the authors say, with the global depolarizing assumption, and claims no proof of accuracy.
haug-accuracy-definition-setup: Section VI, p.5 and the Figure 4 caption, p.6: accuracy is the percentage correct on Ltest = 200 held-out images, with training data drawn at random, 20 repeats per training size. The paper defines its own metric.
haug-noise-fluctuates: Section VI, p.7 (top of the Discussion page): the authors say performance depends strongly on IBM noise and calibration, which fluctuate with time. A limit stated about their own experiment.
haug-limit-exponential-qubits: Section VII, p.7: the paper states that the measurement count grows exponentially in N (refs [41,42]) and that this makes the method currently practical only for few qubits. A limit stated about its own method.
haug-appendixb-test-costs: Appendix B, p.11: the paper describes the inversion test (U_i with inverse U_j, probability of zero) and swap test (two registers, ancilla, controlled SWAP) and states their L^2 measurement count. Description of the comparison methods the paper uses.
rm-kernel-scaling: Abstract p.1 (repeated in Sections IV and VII): the linear scaling is the count NR = srL of the paper's own procedure, and the exponential scaling in qubit number is stated by the authors as the limit of their own method. No speedup claim is in the value.
haug24-scope-tasks: Introduction, p.1: the authors state they apply the DQFIM to unitary learning, quantum control, generative models, excited states and classification. Numerical tests cover unitary learning, control, SSVQE and classification (SM F to J); generative models are an argument in SM H. It states scope only.
haug24-model-test-error: Model section, pp.1-2, Eqs. (1) and (2): the paper defines the cost, the label-operator normalisation and the test error. Its own model definition.
haug24-assumption-ansatz-solves: Model section, p.2: the authors state the assumption that the ansatz can solve the task (a parameter theta_g with zero train and test cost). A stated assumption on what the paper covers.
haug24-three-outcomes: Model section, p.2: the authors define their three outcome classes (local minimum, global minimum without generalization, generalization). Their own classification of outcomes, not a theorem.
haug24-definition1-data-state: Definition 1, p.2, Eq. (3): the data state is the equal mixture of the training states, and training gives only the unitary mapped onto that subspace. The statement is part of the definition and is illustrated by the column example that follows.
haug24-definition2-dqfim-formula: Definition 2, Eq. (4), p.3: the DQFIM is defined by the stated formula, with the derivative with respect to the nth parameter. Matches SM A Eq. (A11).
haug24-dqfim-reduces-to-qfim: DQFIM section p.3 and SM A.2 to A.3, pp.11-12: for L = 1 Eq. (4) is the QFIM by substitution, and the equality of the DQFIM with the QFIM of the purified state is shown by an explicit chain of equalities (Eqs. A16 to A23). The derivation is in the paper.
haug24-effective-dimension-rank: Eqs. (5) and (6), p.3: the paper defines the effective dimension as the rank of the DQFIM (at most M, the matrix size) and the maximal rank RL reached at Mc(L). Its own definitions.
haug24-definition3-overparam: Definition 3, p.3: overparameterization is defined as DL no longer increasing with M. Its own definition.
haug24-definition4-overcomplete: Definition 4, p.3, Eq. (8): overcomplete data is defined as RL no longer increasing with L, with R-infinity reached at the critical Lc. Its own definition.
haug24-theorem2-proof: SM C, pp.15-16: Theorem 2 (restating Theorem 1, p.3) is stated with its conditions (product of exponentials of generators) and proved by an explicit calculation (Eqs. C6 to C12): H-tilde_k lies in the DLA, so Q has a dim(g)-element basis. The proof is written 'in analogy to' ref [59] but uses no cited theorem as a step. Two reductions (RL <= R-infinity, and the data state I/d) are asserted in one sentence each.
haug24-future-work: Conclusion, p.5: the authors name kernel models, noisy systems and quantum natural gradients as work still to be done with the DQFIM. An open direction stated about their own work.
dqfim-numerical-setup: Figure 3 caption, p.4: N = 4 hardware-efficient ansatz, random training states, gradient descent in simulation, median over 10 random target unitaries. The paper's own simulation setup.
dqfim-rank-dla-bound: Theorem 1 (p.3) stated with its conditions (ansatz as a product of exponentials of generators, DLA from nested commutators) and Theorem 2 with proof in SM C, pp.15-16. The proof is explicit and uses no cited theorem as a step (it follows ref [59] in analogy). The reduction to the data state I/d is asserted in one sentence.
he23-graph-encoding-definition: Section 4.1, pp.7-8: the paper defines its own DAG encoding with START and END nodes, one-hot type vector concatenated with the qubit-position vector, gate matrix X and adjacency matrix A.
he23-vgae-encoder-definition: Section 4.2, pp.9-10: the paper defines its own pretext model as a variational graph autoencoder with GIN layers (for isomorphism invariance) and a decoder that rebuilds A, gate types and qubit positions.
he23-pretext-loss: Section 4.2.3, p.10, Eq. (10) (and Section 4, p.6): the pretext loss is the reconstruction loss, optimised as a variational lower bound with a Gaussian-prior KL regulariser by mini-batch gradient descent. Its own definition.
he23-two-schemes: Section 4.3, p.11: GSQAS(URL) freezes the encoder and trains only the predictor; GSQAS(PF) initialises the encoder from the pretext task and trains both. The paper defines its own schemes.
he23-predictor-architecture: Section 4.3, p.10: the predictor takes the average of all node representations and is a two-layer MLP with ReLU and Sigmoid and a batch-norm layer after the first linear layer. Its own definition.
he23-fair-comparison-setup: Section 5, p.11: GQAS is the supervised counterpart with the same predictor, GSQAS(URL) has the same trainable parameter count as GQAS because the encoder is frozen, and all simulations run on TensorCircuit. The paper's own comparison setup.
he23-vqe-task-setup: Section 5.1, pp.11-12, Eq. (11): 6-qubit TFIM with periodic boundary, E0 = -7.7274066. I checked by exact diagonalisation: the ground energy of H = sum ZZ + sum X on a 6-qubit ring is -7.72741.
he23-vqe-search-space: Section 5.1, p.12: search space of ref [29], gate set H, Rx, Ry, Rz, XX, YY, ZZ, 36 gates, maximum depth 10, layerwise generation starting with a Hadamard layer. The paper's own setup.
he23-vqe-sampling-screening: Section 5.1, p.12: 50,000 random circuits, two-stage screening, good circuit if energy below -7.55, predictor label (E - E0)/14. The paper's own setup.
he23-vqe-success-threshold: Section 5.1.3, p.14: energy below -7.7 is taken to mean VQE reached the ground-state energy. The paper defines its own success criterion.
he23-binary-classifier-setup: Section 5.1.2, p.14 and the Table 2 caption: 400 training circuits, filtering of 50,000 random circuits, results averaged over 50 independent runs. The paper's own setup.
he23-predictor-three-settings: Section 5.1.3, p.14: the three settings analysed (probability against number of training circuits, against number of candidate circuits, and average candidate circuits needed). The paper's own protocol.
he23-vqc-task-setup: Section 5.2, pp.16-17: 8-qubit states with CE = 0.15 and 0.45 from the entangled dataset of ref [66], 400 states of each, half train and half test, a PQC then a feedforward net with a 16-neuron hidden layer. The paper's own task setup.
he23-vqc-search-space: Section 5.2, pp.16-17: gate set Rx, Ry, Rz, XX, YY, ZZ, pSWAP, 32 gates, maximum depth 7, and 1000 candidate circuits in the final selection for the Figure 10 runs. The paper's own setup.
he23-sim-only-limit: Section 5, p.11 and Section 6, p.19: all results are numerical simulations on TensorCircuit, and other pretext tasks and other variational algorithms are left as future work. A limit stated about its own work.
gsqas-method: Abstract p.1 and Section 4, pp.6-11: the authors define GSQAS as pre-training a graph encoder on unlabeled circuits with a pretext task, then training the predictor on a few labeled circuit representations. Its own method.
gsqas-scope: Section 6, p.19: simulations cover VQE and VQC, and other pretext tasks and variational algorithms (quantum compiling, QAOA) are left to future work. The value states scope only; the conclusion's claim of superiority is not part of the value.

theory_low.hassanshahi-advantage-condition: Section 5, p.6: the condition beta_Q < beta_C rests on scalings taken from cited work (Havlicek et al., Gentinetta et al. for beta_Q; Bravyi et al. for beta_C). It is an author estimate with coefficients taken by order of magnitude, not a theorem proved in this paper. 'Would be possible for a large number of features' is the authors' interpretation.
theory_low.hassanshahi-min-features-73-140: Section 5, p.7 (after Figure 10): a derived estimate from cited scalings with beta known only to orders of magnitude, as the paper says. Not a proved result or a measurement.
theory_low.hassanshahi-fig10-trend: Read from Figure 10 (p.7): a contour plot of an estimate that itself rests on cited scalings. A value read by eye from a figure is never HIGH. The labelled contours (64 to 148) match the reading.
theory_low.hassanshahi-log-scaling-conclusion: Section 6, p.7: the authors' conclusion from the Section 5 estimate, which uses cited scalings and order-of-magnitude coefficients. The paper itself adds that further noise study could worsen the complexity. An interpretation, not a proved result.
theory_low.haug-rm-linear-in-dataset: Section IV, p.3: the linear count NR = srL is by construction, but the value adds 'a quadratic speedup in contrast to other methods', which is the authors' claim. It holds only at fixed N, s, r and sc. The same paragraph says the cost is exponential in N, and Appendix D shows the advantage starts only above L about 21. No theorem is stated or proved.
theory_low.haug-breakeven-l21: Section IV p.4 and Appendix D p.11: a calculation under assumed s = 8192, r = 8, sc = 5000 and Ltest = Ltrain/5, not a measurement. Using the Appendix D formulas I get a break-even near L = 23, not 21, and a factor about 44 (not 100) at L = 1000. The paper's own numbers are not reproduced exactly.
theory_low.haug-measurement-cost-digits: Section VI, p.6: a calculated estimate under assumed sc = 5000 for the inversion test, not a measured comparison. I recomputed 1.2e8 and 0.8e10 from the stated formulas (ratio about 68, so 'more than 60' holds). The calculation uses 1797 images while Appendix E uses 1790.
theory_low.haug-fig8-crossover: Read from Figure 8 (p.13, rendered and checked): the log-log curves of a calculation. The reading matches the plot (about 1.5e5 and 1e4 at the smallest L, crossing near 20, about 1e8 and 7e9 at 1500). A value read by eye from a figure is never HIGH.
theory_low.haug-qfim-small-c-kernel: textbook, stated not proved (F129): Section III, p.3, Eq. (4) is the second-order fidelity expansion in the QFIM. The paper gives no derivation (it cites [35]) and states no theorem, so it is not a proved result in this paper. Its condition, the limit c to 0, is stated.
theory_low.haug-mnist-9-qubits: Section VII, pp.7-8: the capacity bound rank <= 2^(N+1) - 2 is taken from ref [35]. The N = 9 figure is an inequality check (2^10 - 2 = 1022 >= 784) of an upper bound, not shown to be reachable. No MNIST run was made.
theory_low.haug-npqc-identity-qfim: Section III, p.3 and Appendix A, p.11: that F(theta_r) = I for the NPQC is proved in ref [40] (Haug and Kim, NPQC), cited here, not in this paper. 'Approximate isotropic RBF kernel' rests on ref [38] and the simulations of Figure 2. A result proved elsewhere and cited is not a proved result here.
theory_low.haug-quantum-linear-speedup: Section VII, p.7: a restatement of the linear count with the claim of a quadratic speedup, the authors' interpretation. It holds at fixed N, s, r and sc, and the paper's own Appendix D has the advantage start only above L about 21. No theorem is stated or proved. The classical post-processing L^2 remark is a stated fact, not a proof.
theory_low.haug-mnist-time-estimate: Section VII, p.8: a back-of-envelope estimate under an assumed 5 kHz rate, s = 8192, r = 8 and sc = 1000. No MNIST run was made.
theory_low.haug-appendixh-product-state: Appendix H, p.14 (rendered and checked): a short derivation under |delta theta_n| << 1, equal differences and N to infinity, which the value omits and which makes 'exact' too strong. Eq. (H2) as printed reads (1 + (1/2) cos(delta theta_n)), which is 3/2 at zero shift. The correct overlap is (1 + cos)/2, so the printed formula has an error.
theory_low.haug24-column-argument: Model section, p.2: a worked argument for computational-basis training states. The claim that a trained model guesses the unseen columns at random and so has large test error is not computed. It is not a stated and proved theorem.
theory_low.haug24-effective-dimension-counts: DQFIM section, p.2: D1 = 2d - 2 and Dd = d^2 - 1 are a two-line parameter count (phase and norm removed), and the single-qubit values cite the textbook [67]. 'We require L >= 2 states to generalize' is the authors' inference tied to an unstated test distribution. No theorem is stated and proved here.
theory_low.haug24-commuting-generators-example: DQFIM section, p.2: a worked example stated without derivation (commuting z rotations, W = {|+>,|->}, D1 = Dd = 1 and DL = 0 for {|0>,|1>}). No theorem or proof.
theory_low.haug24-rl-upper-bound-eq7: Eq. (7), p.3 and SM B, pp.14-15: the formula is a count of independent real parameters of an isometry, with the step 'rank of the DQFIM is at most that count' not stated, and one count cited to [75]. 'Tight' rests on numerics (Figure 2b), not on a proof. A bound argued informally.
theory_low.haug24-smb-gain-per-state: SM B, p.15: the difference of the counted RL formula, stated 'for an arbitrary unitary'. Since RL itself is only an upper bound by parameter counting, and equality for a given ansatz is numerical, the gain is not proved here.
theory_low.haug24-poly-dla-corollary: Section DQFIM, p.3, after Theorem 1: the authors' consequence. It needs Lc about 2 R-infinity / R1, which the paper gives only as a numerical estimator (Observation 2), and Mc <= R-infinity. No separate proof. The restricted algebra is cited to [43,45,76].
theory_low.haug24-obs3-ranks-symmetric: Observation 3, p.4 and SM D, p.17: 'we find exactly R1 = 2N - 2, R-infinity = N^2 - 1' is a count (states live in an N-dimensional subspace) with no derivation that the ansatz reaches it. The numerics paragraph (p.4) swaps 'symmetric' and 'non-symmetric' relative to Observation 3. With these ranks 2 R-infinity / R1 = N + 1, not the N given for Lc.
theory_low.haug24-uxy-open-lc1: SM F, pp.20-21: the rank RL = R1 = R-infinity = N^2 for all N is stated with no derivation. Figure 10a gives a simulation for L = 1 only. Not a proved result.
theory_low.haug24-generative-threshold: SM H, p.22: an author inference by mapping fidelity training onto unitary learning with L = 1. No numerical test and no proof.
theory_low.haug24-ssvqe-threshold: SM I, pp.23-24: the paper says 'we argue' that SSVQE is a unitary learning problem with Mc(L) = RL. The generic value is the counted bound of SM B and one simulation (Figure 14) supports it. The priority statement is the authors' own. Not a proved result.

requote.rm-experiment-setup: regraded LOW at the team lead's decision: The Figure 4 caption (p.6) states s = 8192, N = 8, r = 8, Ltest = 200, as do Figures 2, 3 and 9 and the M = 36 NPQC count. Appendix D (p.11) refers to 'the experiment of N = 9 qubits in the main text'. The paper contradicts itself on N, so it does not settle the claim. Likely a slip in Appendix D.; team lead, 2026-11-04, Sprint 15 Manual Validation Q1 option 1 (all 36 as proposed)
